\section{Introduction}

A recurring question in computation is whether a rich language can be reduced to a small instruction set. In real-variable symbolic computation, a natural source language consists of constants and variables together with addition, multiplication, negation, reciprocal, exponential, and logarithm. Exponential and logarithm are conventionally distinct transcendental primitives. We show that, for finite expressions, they can be fused into one two-input transcendental operation without loss of expressive power.

The first fusion is the difference primitive
\[
\Diff(a,b)=e^a-\log b,
\]
and the second is the product primitive
\[
\Prod(a,b)=e^a\log b.
\]
Constants and field operations remain available. Our results are constructive exact compilation theorems: every finite source expression has a finite target expression with the same value in every environment.

For $\Diff$, the essential identities are
\[
e^a=\Diff(a,1),\qquad \log b=1-\Diff(0,b).
\]
For $\Prod$, they are
\[
\log b=\Prod(0,b),\qquad e^a=\Prod(a,e).
\]
The argument proves equivalence of specified finite grammars. It does not prove a Church--Turing thesis for real computation and does not show that every function conventionally called elementary belongs to the grammar. Sine and cosine are not source primitives, and no exact finite exp--log representation of them is obtained.

\section{Languages and total semantics}

\subsection{Total operations}

To give every expression a value on every real input, reciprocal is totalized by $0^{-1}=0$. The real logarithm is taken to satisfy
\[
\log 0=0,\qquad \log x=\log|x|\quad(x\ne0),
\]
where the logarithm on the right is the ordinary positive logarithm. Thus $\log 1=0$ and $\log(e^x)=x$. This convention avoids partial denotations and ensures that compilation also preserves exceptional inputs.

An \emph{environment} is a function $\rho:\N\to\R$ assigning a value to every variable $x_k$.

\begin{definition}[Source expression]
A finite exp--log--field expression is generated by
\[
E ::= c\mid x_k\mid E+E\mid E E\mid -E\mid E^{-1}\mid e^E\mid \log E,
\]
where $c\in\R$ and $k\in\N$. Its denotation is recursively defined by interpreting each constructor as the corresponding total real operation.
\end{definition}

Explicitly,
\begin{align*}
\den{c}{\rho}&=c,& \den{x_k}{\rho}&=\rho(k),\\
\den{A+B}{\rho}&=\den{A}{\rho}+\den{B}{\rho},&
\den{AB}{\rho}&=\den{A}{\rho}\den{B}{\rho},\\
\den{-A}{\rho}&=-\den{A}{\rho},&
\den{A^{-1}}{\rho}&=\den{A}{\rho}^{-1},\\
\den{e^A}{\rho}&=e^{\den{A}{\rho}},&
\den{\log A}{\rho}&=\log\den{A}{\rho}.
\end{align*}
A function $f:\R^n\to\R$ is finitely exp--log representable if one such expression, using the first $n$ variables, equals $f$ at every input.

\begin{definition}[Difference-primitive expression]
A finite difference-primitive expression is generated by
\[
T ::= c\mid x_k\mid T+T\mid TT\mid -T\mid T^{-1}\mid \Diff(T,T),
\]
where
\[
\den{\Diff(A,B)}{\rho}=e^{\den{A}{\rho}}-\log\den{B}{\rho}.
\]
Finite difference-primitive representability means denotation by such an expression at every input.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Product-primitive expression]
A finite product-primitive expression has the same constants, variables, and field nodes, but its sole transcendental constructor is $\Prod$, interpreted by
\[
\den{\Prod(A,B)}{\rho}=e^{\den{A}{\rho}}\log\den{B}{\rho}.
\]
\end{definition}

\section{The difference-primitive compiler}

Define $C_D$ by structural recursion. Constants and variables are unchanged, and the compiler commutes with field operations:
\begin{align*}
C_D(A+B)&=C_D(A)+C_D(B),& C_D(AB)&=C_D(A)C_D(B),\\
C_D(-A)&=-C_D(A),& C_D(A^{-1})&=C_D(A)^{-1}.
\end{align*}
The transcendental clauses are
\[
C_D(e^A)=\Diff(C_D(A),1),
\qquad
C_D(\log A)=1-\Diff(0,C_D(A)).
\]

\begin{theorem}[Exact difference-primitive compilation]
For every finite exp--log--field expression $E$ and every environment $\rho$,
\[
\den{C_D(E)}{\rho}=\den{E}{\rho}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Proceed by structural induction on $E$. Constants and variables are immediate. Addition, multiplication, negation, and reciprocal follow by applying the induction hypotheses to the children and then the corresponding real operation. If $E=e^A$, then
\[
\den{\Diff(C_D(A),1)}{\rho}
=e^{\den{C_D(A)}{\rho}}-\log1
=e^{\den{A}{\rho}}.
\]
If $E=\log A$, then
\begin{align*}
\den{1-\Diff(0,C_D(A))}{\rho}
&=1-\left(e^0-\log\den{C_D(A)}{\rho}\right)\\
&=\log\den{A}{\rho}.
\end{align*}
These cases exhaust the grammar.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Forward representability]
Every finitely exp--log representable function is finitely difference-primitive representable.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Choose a source expression representing the function and compile it. The preceding theorem gives equality at every input.
\end{proof}

For example,
\[
F(x,y)=e^{x+y}+\frac{1}{3-\log y}
\]
compiles to
\[
\Diff(x+y,1)+\frac{1}{3-\bigl(1-\Diff(0,y)\bigr)}.
\]
The equality is exact under the stated total semantics.

\section{Expansion and expressive equivalence}

Define $X_D$ from difference-primitive expressions to source expressions. It recursively preserves all field nodes and replaces
\[
\Diff(A,B)
\quad\text{by}\quad
 e^{X_D(A)}-\log X_D(B).
\]

\begin{theorem}[Exact expansion]
For every finite difference-primitive expression $T$ and environment $\rho$,
\[
\den{X_D(T)}{\rho}=\den{T}{\rho}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Structural induction handles the field cases by congruence. At a $\Diff$ node, expansion is precisely the defining denotation:
\[
\den{e^{X_D(A)}-\log X_D(B)}{\rho}
=e^{\den{A}{\rho}}-\log\den{B}{\rho}.
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Expressive equivalence]
For every finite arity $n$ and function $f:\R^n\to\R$, the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item $f$ is finitely exp--log representable;
\item $f$ is finitely difference-primitive representable.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The forward direction uses compilation. For the reverse direction, choose a difference-primitive expression representing $f$ and expand it. Exact expansion preserves its value everywhere.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Extensional retraction]
For every difference-primitive expression $T$ and environment $\rho$,
\[
\den{C_D(X_D(T))}{\rho}=\den{T}{\rho}.
\]
\end{corollary}

This is extensional rather than syntactic: compiling an expansion can produce a differently shaped tree, but no input distinguishes the computed functions.

\section{The product-primitive compiler}

Define $C_P$ recursively, preserving constants, variables, and field operations. The transcendental clauses are
\[
C_P(\log A)=\Prod(0,C_P(A)),
\qquad
C_P(e^A)=\Prod(C_P(A),e).
\]
They follow from
\[
\Prod(0,b)=e^0\log b=\log b
\]
and
\[
\Prod(a,e)=e^a\log(e)=e^a.
\]

\begin{theorem}[Exact product-primitive compilation]
For every finite exp--log--field expression $E$ and environment $\rho$,
\[
\den{C_P(E)}{\rho}=\den{E}{\rho}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Induct structurally on $E$. Field cases are homomorphic. The logarithm case uses $e^0=1$, and the exponential case uses $\log(e)=1$. The induction hypothesis identifies each compiled argument with its source denotation.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Product-primitive representability]
Every finitely exp--log representable function is finitely product-primitive representable.
\end{corollary}

A converse can be obtained by replacing every $\Prod(A,B)$ with $e^A\log B$, although that direction is not required for the compilation result.

\section{Monomials and Horner polynomials}

Fix a variable $x_k$ and define
\[
M_{k,0}=1,
\qquad
M_{k,m+1}=x_kM_{k,m}.
\]

\begin{lemma}[Monomial evaluation]
For every $k,m\in\N$ and environment $\rho$,
\[
\den{M_{k,m}}{\rho}=\rho(k)^m.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Induct on $m$. The base case is $1=\rho(k)^0$. At a successor, multiply the induction hypothesis by $\rho(k)$ and use the recursive law for powers.
\end{proof}

Let $A=[a_0,a_1,\ldots,a_m]$ list coefficients in ascending degree order. Define numerical Horner evaluation by
\[
H(x,[])=0,
\qquad
H(x,a::A)=a+xH(x,A).
\]
Define source expressions by
\[
Q_k([])=0,
\qquad
Q_k(a::A)=a+x_kQ_k(A).
\]

\begin{lemma}[Horner expression evaluation]
For every coefficient list $A$, index $k$, and environment $\rho$,
\[
\den{Q_k(A)}{\rho}=H(\rho(k),A).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Induct on the list. Both empty values are zero. In the nonempty case, substitute the induction hypothesis inside $a+\rho(k)(\cdot)$.
\end{proof}

Unfolding the recursion yields
\[
H(x,[a_0,\ldots,a_m])
=a_0+x\bigl(a_1+x(\cdots+xa_m)\cdots\bigr)
=\sum_{j=0}^m a_jx^j.
\]

\begin{theorem}[Polynomial difference-primitive representation]
For every finite real coefficient list $A$, the polynomial $x\mapsto H(x,A)$ has the explicit finite difference-primitive representation $C_D(Q_0(A))$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The Horner lemma identifies the source expression with the numerical polynomial, and exact difference-primitive compilation preserves its value.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Polynomial product-primitive representation]
For every finite real coefficient list $A$, the polynomial $x\mapsto H(x,A)$ has the explicit finite product-primitive representation $C_P(Q_0(A))$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Combine Horner evaluation with exact product-primitive compilation.
\end{proof}

The polynomial source trees contain no transcendental nodes, so their compiled forms need none. Their role is constructive: they provide a canonical family and connect the compilers with a standard evaluation algorithm.

\section{Algorithms and complexity}

Both compilers are single-pass tree transformations. A depth-first implementation compiles each child and emits a constant-sized target fragment for the parent. If $|E|$ is the number of source nodes and built descendants are not recopied, each compiler takes $O(|E|)$ time and produces $O(|E|)$ target nodes. The recursion stack uses $O(h)$ space for source-tree height $h$. With directed acyclic graphs, memoization preserves sharing and gives time linear in the number of distinct nodes.

For a list of $m+1$ coefficients, Horner evaluation uses $m$ multiplications and $m$ additions. It takes $O(m)$ time and can be implemented iteratively with $O(1)$ auxiliary storage.

Numerical grid testing can compare source and target evaluators and expose implementation mistakes, but finite samples do not establish equality on all reals. Floating-point comparisons also require tolerances and care near overflow or singular-looking expressions.

\section{Worked examples}

\begin{example}[Nested difference compilation]
For
\[
F(x,y)=e^{x+y}+\frac{1}{3-\log y},
\]
the output is
\[
F_D(x,y)=\Diff(x+y,1)+\frac{1}{3-\bigl(1-\Diff(0,y)\bigr)}.
\]
Since $\Diff(x+y,1)=e^{x+y}$ and $1-\Diff(0,y)=\log y$, the functions agree everywhere under total semantics.
\end{example}

\begin{example}[Product compilation]
For
\[
G(x)=e^{x^2}+\log(1+x^2),
\]
the product compiler gives
\[
G_P(x)=\Prod(x^2,e)+\Prod(0,1+x^2).
\]
The first term is $e^{x^2}$ and the second is $\log(1+x^2)$.
\end{example}

\begin{example}[Coefficient-list polynomial]
The list $[2,-3,0,5]$ has Horner value
\[
2+x\bigl(-3+x(0+5x)\bigr)=2-3x+5x^3.
\]
It is accepted by both target languages because they retain constants and field operations.
\end{example}

\section{Applications and interpretation}

A symbolic or hardware language may expose one transcendental gate type while retaining arithmetic. The compilation theorems show that either $\Diff$ or $\Prod$ covers the entire finite exp--log source language. A front end can retain conventional notation while a back end lowers both transcendental operations to a uniform gate.

Expression-search systems face a combinatorial choice of primitives. Replacing two transcendental constructors with one simplifies the vocabulary, although it can enlarge trees. Expressive equivalence ensures that no function already finitely expressible in the source language is lost. Search efficiency and regularization remain empirical issues.

Repeated instances of a common nonlinear gate can also be composed with arithmetic layers in differentiable architectures. The results isolate exact representability; they do not address training, parameter efficiency, or universal approximation.

The theorems concern exact real semantics, not floating-point stability. The representation $\log b=1-\Diff(0,b)$ can involve cancellation, exponentials may overflow, and behavior near zero may be sensitive. Practical compilation should therefore add range reduction, simplification, and error analysis.

\section{Scope, limitations, and future work}

``Single operator'' means one \emph{kind} of transcendental node, not one occurrence. A target tree can contain many finite occurrences combined with field operations.

Finite expression definability is also narrower than computability. A computable function may be specified by a limit, differential equation, infinite series, or algorithm without having a finite expression in this grammar.

Sine and cosine lie outside the source language. The familiar identity
\[
\sin x=\frac{e^{ix}-e^{-ix}}{2i}
\]
uses complex constants and complex exponentials and therefore does not supply a real exp--log expression. A plausible global obstruction is that sine has the infinite discrete zero set $\{k\pi:k\in\mathbb Z\}$, whereas one-variable functions definable in tame expansions of the real field should have zero sets made from finitely many points and intervals. Establishing the necessary tameness result lies beyond structural compilation.

Approximation is separate from equality. On compact intervals, polynomial approximation can supply target expressions arbitrarily close to sine or cosine because polynomials already belong to both target languages. The expression depends on the interval and tolerance, and no exact global identity follows.

Concrete future directions include:
\begin{enumerate}
\item proving global trigonometric non-representability through a suitable one-variable tameness theorem;
\item deciding whether an exp--log expression can agree exactly with sine on any nonempty open interval;
\item obtaining quantitative expression-size bounds for uniform approximation of sine and cosine on compact intervals;
\item deriving sharp linear compiler-size bounds under a fixed node-cost model and studying the effect of sharing;
\item using trigonometric non-representability to test the stronger thesis that every computable real function has an exact finite single-operator expression;
\item analyzing numerical error and constructing range-sensitive lowering rules;
\item extending explicit polynomial compilation to sparse and dense multivariate representations.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Conclusion}

Finite expressions generated by real constants, variables, field operations, exponential, and total logarithm admit exact compilation to a language with one transcendental gate. For $\Diff(a,b)=e^a-\log b$, the identities $e^a=\Diff(a,1)$ and $\log b=1-\Diff(0,b)$ yield a semantics-preserving compiler, while expansion proves full expressive equivalence. For $\Prod(a,b)=e^a\log b$, the identities $\log b=\Prod(0,b)$ and $e^a=\Prod(a,e)$ yield a second exact compiler. Monomials and Horner polynomials provide explicit constructive examples.

The result is a precise instruction-set theorem for a finite exp--log language. Its strength is exactness over every finite expression tree, and its boundary is equally precise: it neither supplies exact trigonometric expressions nor establishes universality for all computable real functions.

from typing import Callable, Mapping, Sequence, Union

class Var:

def total_log(x: float) -> float:
    """Total real logarithm: log(0)=0 and log(x)=log(abs(x)) otherwise."""
    return 0.0 if x == 0.0 else math.log(abs(x))


def total_inv(x: float) -> float:
    """Total reciprocal with 0 inverse defined as 0."""
    return 0.0 if x == 0.0 else 1.0 / x


def evaluate(expr: Expr, env: Environment) -> float:
    """Evaluate a source or compiled expression tree."""
    if isinstance(expr, Const):

        return env[expr.name]
    if isinstance(expr, Unary):
        value = evaluate(expr.child, env)

            "exp": math.exp,

    right = evaluate(expr.right, env)
    if expr.op == "add":

    if expr.op == "mul":

    if expr.op == "D":

    if expr.op == "P":
        return math.exp(left) * total_log(right)

Begin with two apparently different nonlinear operations, $e^x$ and $\log x$. The central question is an instruction-set question: can one two-input gate contain both operations without losing any finite formula built from them?

The answer is yes for each of the gates

$$
D(a,b)=e^a-\log b, \qquad P(a,b)=e^a\log b.
$$

## 1. Touch the identities

The explorer below lets you vary inputs in nested formulas. Three independently evaluated curves are overlaid: the original exp–log expression, its $D$-gate translation, and its $P$-gate translation. Try $y=1$, where logarithm vanishes, and move toward $y=0$ to see the chosen total semantics at work.

{{interactive_demo:0}}

<details><summary><strong>Reveal the two-line algebra behind the difference gate</strong></summary>

Since $\log 1=0$ and $e^0=1$,

$$
D(a,1)=e^a, \qquad 1-D(0,b)=\log b.
$$

A compiler replaces every exponential and logarithm node by these templates, recursively translating the children first.
</details>

<details><summary><strong>Reveal the product-gate identities</strong></summary>

Since $e^0=1$ and $\log e=1$,

$$
P(0,b)=\log b, \qquad P(a,e)=e^a.
$$

Thus the product gate supports a parallel exact compiler.
</details>

## 2. Follow the compiler

Compilation is a walk over a finite expression tree. Arithmetic nodes retain their kind; only transcendental nodes are rewritten. Read the algorithm, then run the numerical demonstration on a nested example and on the polynomial $2-3x+5x^3$.

Use structural induction. Leaves are unchanged. If translated child expressions preserve their values, applying the same arithmetic operation preserves the parent's value. The only new cases are exponential and logarithm, discharged by the identities above. This proves equality for every input, not merely for the displayed samples.
</details>

## 3. See the cost of translation

The target tree grows only linearly because each source node produces a constant-size fragment. Hover over the generated bars to inspect node counts under an illustrative cost convention.

{{visualization:0}}

<details><summary><strong>Complexity details</strong></summary>

For a tree with $N$ nodes and height $h$, a depth-first compiler runs in $O(N)$ time, emits $O(N)$ nodes, and uses $O(h)$ stack space. If the input is a directed acyclic graph, memoization can preserve shared subexpressions and remain linear in the number of distinct nodes.
</details>

## 4. Build a polynomial without transcendental nodes

Horner's recurrence for ascending coefficients is

$$
H(x,[])=0, \qquad H(x,a::A)=a+xH(x,A).
$$

It evaluates a degree-$m$ polynomial with $m$ additions and $m$ multiplications. Because arithmetic is shared by all three languages, every such polynomial already belongs to both single-gate languages.

{{algorithm:1}}

## 5. Understand the boundary

The exact theorem concerns finite exp–log–field expressions. It does **not** say that every computable real function has such an expression. Sine is a revealing test: its zeros form the infinite discrete set $\{k\pi:k\in\mathbb Z\}$, suggesting a conflict with the tame zero sets expected from one-variable real exp–log terms.

Approximation is different. On compact intervals, polynomial approximations bring sine and cosine into the single-gate languages to any prescribed positive tolerance, while exact global equality remains open here.

<details><summary><strong>Research questions to take away</strong></summary>

Can global or interval-wise non-representability of sine be proved? What are sharp compiler-size constants? How does exact algebraic compilation interact with floating-point stability? These questions separate syntax, definability, approximation, and practical evaluation.
</details>

# Exact compilation to the catalog's single EML operator

This file builds on `EMLExpr` and `EMLOnlyExpr` from the existing catalog.  It
proves that every finite expression made from real constants, variables, field
operations, `Real.exp`, and Mathlib's total `Real.log` can be compiled to an

not a consequence of the elementary identities proved here.

namespace EMLSingleOperator

open EMLExpr EMLOnlyExpr

def compile : EMLExpr → EMLOnlyExpr
  | .const c => .const c
  | .var n => .var n
  | .add p q => .add (compile p) (compile q)
  | .mul p q => .mul (compile p) (compile q)
  | .neg p => .neg (compile p)
  | .inv p => .inv (compile p)
  | .exp p => .eml (compile p) (.const 1)
  | .log p => .add (.const 1) (.neg (.eml (.const 0) (compile p)))

totalized exceptional inputs of inverse and logarithm. -/
theorem compile_eval (e : EMLExpr) (env : ℕ → ℝ) :
    (compile e).eval env = e.eval env := by
  induction e with
  | const c => rfl
  | var n => rfl
  | add p q hp hq => simp [compile, EMLExpr.eval, EMLOnlyExpr.eval, hp, hq]
  | mul p q hp hq => simp [compile, EMLExpr.eval, EMLOnlyExpr.eval, hp, hq]
  | neg p hp => simp [compile, EMLExpr.eval, EMLOnlyExpr.eval, hp]
  | inv p hp => simp [compile, EMLExpr.eval, EMLOnlyExpr.eval, hp]
  | exp p hp => simp [compile, EMLExpr.eval, EMLOnlyExpr.eval, hp]
  | log p hp => simp [compile, EMLExpr.eval, EMLOnlyExpr.eval, hp]

represented by a finite expression using only the catalog's EML transcendental
node and field operations. -/
theorem representable_to_single_operator {n : ℕ} {f : (Fin n → ℝ) → ℝ}

  rcases hf with ⟨e, he⟩
  refine ⟨compile e, ?_⟩
  intro x
  rw [compile_eval, he]

/-- Embed a single-operator expression back into the exp-log grammar. -/
def expand : EMLOnlyExpr → EMLExpr
  | .const c => .const c
  | .var n => .var n
  | .add p q => .add (expand p) (expand q)
  | .mul p q => .mul (expand p) (expand q)
  | .neg p => .neg (expand p)
  | .inv p => .inv (expand p)
  | .eml p q => .add (.exp (expand p)) (.neg (.log (expand q)))

    (expand e).eval env = e.eval env := by
  induction e with
  | const c => rfl
  | var n => rfl
  | add p q hp hq => simp [expand, EMLExpr.eval, EMLOnlyExpr.eval, hp, hq]
  | mul p q hp hq => simp [expand, EMLExpr.eval, EMLOnlyExpr.eval, hp, hq]
  | neg p hp => simp [expand, EMLExpr.eval, EMLOnlyExpr.eval, hp]
  | inv p hp => simp [expand, EMLExpr.eval, EMLOnlyExpr.eval, hp]
  | eml p q hp hq =>
      simp [expand, EMLExpr.eval, EMLOnlyExpr.eval, hp, hq, sub_eq_add_neg]

theorem representable_iff_single_operator {n : ℕ} {f : (Fin n → ℝ) → ℝ} :

  constructor
  · exact representable_to_single_operator
  · rintro ⟨e, he⟩
    refine ⟨expand e, ?_⟩
    intro x
    rw [expand_eval, he]

  | m + 1 => .mul (.var k) (monomialExpr k m)

theorem monomialExpr_eval (k m : ℕ) (env : ℕ → ℝ) :
    (monomialExpr k m).eval env = env k ^ m := by
  induction m with

    (polynomialExpr k as).eval env = polynomialValue (env k) as := by
  induction as with
  | nil => rfl
  | cons a as ih => simp [polynomialExpr, polynomialValue, EMLExpr.eval, ih]

theorem polynomial_single_operator (as : List ℝ) :
    EMLOnlyRepresentable (fun x : Fin 1 → ℝ => polynomialValue (x 0) as) := by
  refine ⟨compile (polynomialExpr 0 as), ?_⟩

  rw [compile_eval, polynomialExpr_eval]
  have hx : emlEnv x 0 = x (0 : Fin 1) := emlEnv_coe x (0 : Fin 1)
  rw [hx]

  refine ⟨.eml (.var 0) (.const 1), ?_⟩

    EMLOnlyRepresentable (fun x : Fin 1 → ℝ => Real.log (x 0)) := by
  refine ⟨.add (.const 1) (.neg (.eml (.const 0) (.var 0))), ?_⟩
  intro x
  have hx : emlEnv x 0 = x (0 : Fin 1) := emlEnv_coe x (0 : Fin 1)
  simp [EMLOnlyExpr.eval, hx]

theorem compile_expand_eval (e : EMLOnlyExpr) (env : ℕ → ℝ) :
    (compile (expand e)).eval env = e.eval env := by
  rw [compile_eval, expand_eval]

compiler verify that version independently, without changing the established
catalog definition. -/

/-- Expressions whose sole transcendental primitive is
`productEML(a,b) = exp(a) * log(b)`. -/
inductive ProductEMLExpr : Type where
  | const (c : ℝ)
  | var (n : ℕ)
  | add (p q : ProductEMLExpr)
  | mul (p q : ProductEMLExpr)
  | neg (p : ProductEMLExpr)
  | inv (p : ProductEMLExpr)
  | productEML (p q : ProductEMLExpr)
  deriving Inhabited

namespace ProductEMLExpr

/-- Total denotational semantics of the product-primitive grammar. -/
def eval : ProductEMLExpr → (ℕ → ℝ) → ℝ
  | .const c, _ => c
  | .var n, env => env n
  | .add p q, env => p.eval env + q.eval env
  | .mul p q, env => p.eval env * q.eval env
  | .neg p, env => -(p.eval env)
  | .inv p, env => (p.eval env)⁻¹

/-- Compile exp-log-field expressions to the product primitive.  Here
`log(b) = productEML(0,b)` and
`exp(a) = productEML(a,exp(1))`, since `log(exp(1)) = 1`. -/
def compileProduct : EMLExpr → ProductEMLExpr
  | .const c => .const c
  | .var n => .var n
  | .add p q => .add (compileProduct p) (compileProduct q)
  | .mul p q => .mul (compileProduct p) (compileProduct q)
  | .neg p => .neg (compileProduct p)
  | .inv p => .inv (compileProduct p)
  | .exp p => .productEML (compileProduct p) (.const (Real.exp 1))
  | .log p => .productEML (.const 0) (compileProduct p)

theorem compileProduct_eval (e : EMLExpr) (env : ℕ → ℝ) :
    (compileProduct e).eval env = e.eval env := by
  induction e with
  | const c => rfl
  | var n => rfl
  | add p q hp hq => simp [compileProduct, ProductEMLExpr.eval, EMLExpr.eval, hp, hq]
  | mul p q hp hq => simp [compileProduct, ProductEMLExpr.eval, EMLExpr.eval, hp, hq]
  | neg p hp => simp [compileProduct, ProductEMLExpr.eval, EMLExpr.eval, hp]
  | inv p hp => simp [compileProduct, ProductEMLExpr.eval, EMLExpr.eval, hp]
  | exp p hp =>
      simp [compileProduct, ProductEMLExpr.eval, EMLExpr.eval, hp]
  | log p hp =>
      simp [compileProduct, ProductEMLExpr.eval, EMLExpr.eval, hp]

/-- Representability using the product primitive. -/
def ProductEMLRepresentable {n : ℕ} (f : (Fin n → ℝ) → ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∃ e : ProductEMLExpr, ∀ x : Fin n → ℝ, e.eval (emlEnv x) = f x

/-- Every function in the exp-log-field grammar is exactly representable using
`exp(a) * log(b)` as its only transcendental primitive. -/
theorem representable_to_product_operator {n : ℕ} {f : (Fin n → ℝ) → ℝ}
    (hf : EMLRepresentable f) : ProductEMLRepresentable f := by
  rcases hf with ⟨e, he⟩
  refine ⟨compileProduct e, ?_⟩
  intro x
  rw [compileProduct_eval, he]

representation. -/
theorem polynomial_product_operator (as : List ℝ) :
    ProductEMLRepresentable (fun x : Fin 1 → ℝ => polynomialValue (x 0) as) := by
  refine ⟨compileProduct (polynomialExpr 0 as), ?_⟩
  intro x
  rw [compileProduct_eval, polynomialExpr_eval]
  have hx : emlEnv x 0 = x (0 : Fin 1) := emlEnv_coe x (0 : Fin 1)
  rw [hx]

  "future_directions": "# Future directions

The exact compiler in `Catalog/Applications/EML/SingleOperatorCompilation.lean`
settles the equivalence of the catalog's finite `{exp, log, field operations}`

following are concrete, falsifiable next questions.

   one-variable consequence of o-minimality of the real exponential field:
   the zero set of an exp-log term is a finite union of points and intervals,
   whereas the zeros of sine form an infinite discrete set.  A single explicit

   tested by formalizing analytic continuation/differential-algebraic
   invariants.  An exact term on one specified open interval falsifies it.

   `[a,b]` and every positive `ε`, there is an `EMLOnlyExpr` whose evaluation is
   uniformly within `ε` of sine (respectively cosine) on that interval.
   Explicit bounds on expression size as a function of `b-a` and `ε` would
   make this quantitative; failure at one concrete interval and tolerance
   falsifies it.

   there are explicit constants `A,B` such that the target syntax-tree size is
   at most `A` times the source size plus `B`; moreover, the optimal leading
   constant for the difference primitive is `3`.  A family of source terms
   whose compiled size exceeds the proposed bound, or a compiler with a
   strictly smaller asymptotic constant, falsifies the corresponding part.

5. **Computability thesis counterexample.** Under any standard representation

    "demo": "#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Numerical demonstrations of exact single-operator compilation.

The script builds finite expression trees, compiles them to either
D(a,b) = exp(a) - log(b) or P(a,b) = exp(a) * log(b), and compares source
and target evaluations on deterministic sample grids. Python floating-point
arithmetic is used only to illustrate the exact real identities.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass
import math
from typing import Callable, Mapping, Sequence, Union


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Const:
    value: float


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Var:
    name: str


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Unary:
    op: str
    child: "Expr"


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Binary:
    op: str
    left: "Expr"
    right: "Expr"


Expr = Union[Const, Var, Unary, Binary]
Environment = Mapping[str, float]


def total_log(x: float) -> float:
    """Total real logarithm: log(0)=0 and log(x)=log(abs(x)) otherwise."""
    return 0.0 if x == 0.0 else math.log(abs(x))


def total_inv(x: float) -> float:
    """Total reciprocal with 0 inverse defined as 0."""
    return 0.0 if x == 0.0 else 1.0 / x


def evaluate(expr: Expr, env: Environment) -> float:
    """Evaluate a source or compiled expression tree."""
    if isinstance(expr, Const):
        return expr.value
    if isinstance(expr, Var):
        return env[expr.name]
    if isinstance(expr, Unary):
        value = evaluate(expr.child, env)
        operations: dict[str, Callable[[float], float]] = {
            "neg": lambda z: -z,
            "inv": total_inv,
            "exp": math.exp,
            "log": total_log,
        }
        return operations[expr.op](value)
    left = evaluate(expr.left, env)
    right = evaluate(expr.right, env)
    if expr.op == "add":
        return left + right
    if expr.op == "mul":
        return left * right
    if expr.op == "D":
        return math.exp(left) - total_log(right)
    if expr.op == "P":
        return math.exp(left) * total_log(right)
    raise ValueError(f"unknown binary operation: {expr.op}")


def add(left: Expr, right: Expr) -> Expr:
    return Binary("add", left, right)


def mul(left: Expr, right: Expr) -> Expr:
    return Binary("mul", left, right)


def neg(child: Expr) -> Expr:
    return Unary("neg", child)


def inv(child: Expr) -> Expr:
    return Unary("inv", child)


def exp(child: Expr) -> Expr:
    return Unary("exp", child)


def log(child: Expr) -> Expr:
    return Unary("log", child)


def compile_difference(expr: Expr) -> Expr:
    """Compile exp/log nodes to D(a,b)=exp(a)-log(b)."""
    if isinstance(expr, (Const, Var)):
        return expr
    if isinstance(expr, Binary):
        if expr.op not in {"add", "mul"}:
            raise ValueError("source tree must use only source operations")
        return Binary(
            expr.op,
            compile_difference(expr.left),
            compile_difference(expr.right),
        )
    child = compile_difference(expr.child)
    if expr.op in {"neg", "inv"}:
        return Unary(expr.op, child)
    if expr.op == "exp":
        return Binary("D", child, Const(1.0))
    if expr.op == "log":
        # 1 - D(0, child), represented using addition and negation.
        return add(Const(1.0), neg(Binary("D", Const(0.0), child)))
    raise ValueError(f"unknown source operation: {expr.op}")


def compile_product(expr: Expr) -> Expr:
    """Compile exp/log nodes to P(a,b)=exp(a)*log(b)."""
    if isinstance(expr, (Const, Var)):
        return expr
    if isinstance(expr, Binary):
        if expr.op not in {"add", "mul"}:
            raise ValueError("source tree must use only source operations")
        return Binary(expr.op, compile_product(expr.left), compile_product(expr.right))
    child = compile_product(expr.child)
    if expr.op in {"neg", "inv"}:
        return Unary(expr.op, child)
    if expr.op == "exp":
        return Binary("P", child, Const(math.e))
    if expr.op == "log":
        return Binary("P", Const(0.0), child)
    raise ValueError(f"unknown source operation: {expr.op}")


def expand_difference(expr: Expr) -> Expr:
    """Expand every D node back to exp(left)-log(right)."""
    if isinstance(expr, (Const, Var)):
        return expr
    if isinstance(expr, Unary):
        return Unary(expr.op, expand_difference(expr.child))
    left = expand_difference(expr.left)
    right = expand_difference(expr.right)
    if expr.op == "D":
        return add(exp(left), neg(log(right)))
    return Binary(expr.op, left, right)


def horner(coefficients: Sequence[float], x: float) -> float:
    """Evaluate ascending-order coefficients by Horner's method."""
    accumulator = 0.0
    for coefficient in reversed(coefficients):
        accumulator = coefficient + x * accumulator
    return accumulator


def polynomial_expr(coefficients: Sequence[float], variable: str = "x") -> Expr:
    """Build the Horner expression for ascending-order coefficients."""
    result: Expr = Const(0.0)
    x = Var(variable)
    for coefficient in reversed(coefficients):
        result = add(Const(coefficient), mul(x, result))
    return result


def node_count(expr: Expr) -> int:
    """Count syntax-tree nodes."""
    if isinstance(expr, (Const, Var)):
        return 1
    if isinstance(expr, Unary):
        return 1 + node_count(expr.child)
    return 1 + node_count(expr.left) + node_count(expr.right)


def close(left: float, right: float) -> bool:
    return math.isclose(left, right, rel_tol=1e-12, abs_tol=1e-12)


def demonstrate_compilers() -> None:
    """Compare source, difference-target, product-target, and expansion."""
    x, y = Var("x"), Var("y")
    source = add(exp(add(x, y)), inv(add(Const(3.0), neg(log(y)))))
    difference = compile_difference(source)
    product = compile_product(source)
    expanded = expand_difference(difference)

    print("Nested exp-log expression")
    print(f"  source nodes: {node_count(source)}")
    print(f"  difference-target nodes: {node_count(difference)}")
    print(f"  product-target nodes: {node_count(product)}")
    print("  x       y        source              D target            P target")
    for xv in (-1.25, -0.2, 0.75, 1.4):
        for yv in (0.0, 0.4, 1.0, 2.5):
            env = {"x": xv, "y": yv}
            values = [
                evaluate(source, env),
                evaluate(difference, env),
                evaluate(product, env),
                evaluate(expanded, env),
            ]
            assert all(close(values[0], value) for value in values[1:])
            print(f"  {xv:5.2f}  {yv:5.2f}  {values[0]:18.12g}  "
                  f"{values[1]:18.12g}  {values[2]:18.12g}")


def demonstrate_polynomial() -> None:
    """Show exact Horner representation of 2-3x+5x^3."""
    coefficients = [2.0, -3.0, 0.0, 5.0]
    expression = polynomial_expr(coefficients)
    difference = compile_difference(expression)
    product = compile_product(expression)
    print("\nHorner polynomial 2 - 3x + 5x^3")
    print("  x       direct              Horner/tree         D target            P target")
    for x in (-2.0, -0.5, 0.0, 0.75, 1.5):
        direct = 2.0 - 3.0 * x + 5.0 * x**3
        values = (
            horner(coefficients, x),
            evaluate(expression, {"x": x}),
            evaluate(difference, {"x": x}),
            evaluate(product, {"x": x}),
        )
        assert all(close(direct, value) for value in values)
        print(f"  {x:5.2f}  {direct:18.12g}  {values[1]:18.12g}  "
              f"{values[2]:18.12g}  {values[3]:18.12g}")


def main() -> None:
    demonstrate_compilers()
    demonstrate_polynomial()
    print("\nAll numerical comparisons agree within floating-point tolerance.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
"

import Mathlib

/-!
# Algebraic foundations for graded encoding systems

This file isolates the algebraic interface needed by multilinear Diffie--Hellman
reductions. It builds on Mathlib's `CommMonoid`; no new group operation is
introduced. Levels are tracked by the type of each encoding.
-/

open scoped BigOperators

namespace Cryptography.GradedEncoding

universe u v

/-- A graded encoding system over an existing commutative monoid. Multiplication
adds levels and agrees with multiplication of plaintexts on canonical encodings. -/
structure System (R : Type u) [CommMonoid R] where
  Code : ℕ → Type v
  encode : (level : ℕ) → R → Code level
  mul : {i j : ℕ} → Code i → Code j → Code (i + j)
  mul_encode : ∀ {i j : ℕ} (x y : R),
    mul (encode i x) (encode j y) = encode (i + j) (x * y)

namespace System

variable {R : Type u} [CommMonoid R]

/-- Canonical multilinear evaluation of plaintext inputs. The result level is
exactly the number of inputs. -/
def multilinearEval (S : System R) (xs : List R) : S.Code xs.length :=
  S.encode xs.length xs.prod

/-- Multiplying a canonical evaluation by one more level-one input produces
the product at the incremented level. -/
theorem multilinearEval_step (S : System R) (xs : List R) (x : R) :
    S.mul (S.multilinearEval xs) (S.encode 1 x) =
      S.encode (xs.length + 1) (xs.prod * x) := by
  exact S.mul_encode xs.prod x

/-- A canonical `k`-multilinear Diffie--Hellman source challenge. -/
structure MDHSource (R : Type u) (k : ℕ) where
  exponents : Fin k → R

/-- The multilinear Diffie--Hellman target in the plaintext monoid. -/
def MDHSource.target {k : ℕ} (C : MDHSource R k) : R :=
  ∏ i, C.exponents i

/-- The public graded transcript associated with a source challenge. -/
structure MDHTranscript (S : System R) (k : ℕ) where
  publicEncoding : Fin k → S.Code 1
  targetEncoding : S.Code k

/-- Canonically encode a multilinear Diffie--Hellman source challenge. -/
def encodeChallenge (S : System R) {k : ℕ} (C : MDHSource R k) : MDHTranscript S k where
  publicEncoding := fun i => S.encode 1 (C.exponents i)
  targetEncoding := S.encode k C.target

/-- The challenge target canonically encodes the product of all source exponents. -/
theorem encodeChallenge_target (S : System R) {k : ℕ} (C : MDHSource R k) :
    (S.encodeChallenge C).targetEncoding =
      S.encode k (∏ i, C.exponents i) := by
  simp [encodeChallenge, MDHSource.target]

end System
end Cryptography.GradedEncoding

import Cryptography.LWE.OperationalSecurity

/-!
# Security reductions for multilinear graded encodings

The reduction layer is independent of any particular graded-encoding candidate.
A decisional multilinear Diffie--Hellman game is represented by its two finite
transcript distributions. A perfect reduction is an equivalence of transcript
spaces preserving both distributions pointwise. The main theorem proves exact
preservation of every deterministic distinguisher's advantage and transfers any
source hardness bound to the graded target game.
-/

open Finset

noncomputable section

namespace Cryptography.GradedEncoding

/-- A finite two-world decisional game. `false` is the random world and `true`
is the real multilinear Diffie--Hellman world. -/
structure DecisionGame (Ω : Type*) [Fintype Ω] where
  experiment : LWEOperational.EncryptionExperiment Ω

namespace DecisionGame

variable {Ω : Type*} [Fintype Ω]

/-- Acceptance probability of a deterministic distinguisher in one world. -/
def acceptance (G : DecisionGame Ω) (b : Bool) (A : Ω → Bool) : ℝ :=
  ∑ x with A x = true, (G.experiment.challenge b).mass x

/-- Absolute distinguishing advantage. -/
def advantage (G : DecisionGame Ω) (A : Ω → Bool) : ℝ :=
  |G.acceptance true A - G.acceptance false A|

/-- Advantage is unchanged when the two challenge worlds are interchanged. -/
theorem advantage_swap (G : DecisionGame Ω) (A : Ω → Bool) :
    |G.acceptance false A - G.acceptance true A| = G.advantage A := by
  exact abs_sub_comm _ _

end DecisionGame

variable {Source Target : Type*} [Fintype Source] [Fintype Target]

/-- A perfect, lossless reduction between finite decisional games. The transcript
equivalence is executable, while `mass_preserving` states exact simulation of
both challenge worlds. -/
structure PerfectReduction (source : DecisionGame Source)
    (target : DecisionGame Target) where
  transcriptEquiv : Source ≃ Target
  mass_preserving : ∀ (b : Bool) (x : Source),
    (target.experiment.challenge b).mass (transcriptEquiv x) =
      (source.experiment.challenge b).mass x

namespace PerfectReduction

variable {source : DecisionGame Source} {target : DecisionGame Target}

/-- Turn a target-game distinguisher into a source-game distinguisher. -/
def reduce (red : PerfectReduction source target) (A : Target → Bool) : Source → Bool :=
  A ∘ red.transcriptEquiv

/-- Perfect simulation preserves acceptance probability in each challenge world. -/
theorem acceptance_eq (red : PerfectReduction source target)
    (A : Target → Bool) (b : Bool) :
    source.acceptance b (red.reduce A) = target.acceptance b A := by
  rw [DecisionGame.acceptance, DecisionGame.acceptance]
  simp only [Finset.sum_filter]
  rw [← Equiv.sum_comp red.transcriptEquiv
    (fun y => if A y = true then (target.experiment.challenge b).mass y else 0)]
  apply Finset.sum_congr rfl
  intro x _
  simp only [reduce, Function.comp_apply]
  split_ifs with h
  · rw [red.mass_preserving]
  · rfl

/-- **Exact reduction theorem.** Every target distinguisher has exactly the same
advantage after reduction to the source multilinear Diffie--Hellman game. -/
theorem advantage_eq (red : PerfectReduction source target) (A : Target → Bool) :
    source.advantage (red.reduce A) = target.advantage A := by
  simp only [DecisionGame.advantage]
  rw [red.acceptance_eq A true, red.acceptance_eq A false]

/-- **Multilinear Diffie--Hellman hardness transfer.** If all source-game
adversaries have advantage at most `ε`, then all target graded-encoding
adversaries do as well. -/
theorem hardness_transfer (red : PerfectReduction source target) (ε : ℝ)
    (sourceHard : ∀ B : Source → Bool, source.advantage B ≤ ε) :
    ∀ A : Target → Bool, target.advantage A ≤ ε := by
  intro A
  rw [← red.advantage_eq A]
  exact sourceHard (red.reduce A)

/-- A strict target-game advantage yields a strict source-game advantage, the
contrapositive form used to turn an attack into an MDH solver. -/
theorem attack_to_source (red : PerfectReduction source target) (ε : ℝ)
    (A : Target → Bool) (attack : ε < target.advantage A) :
    ε < source.advantage (red.reduce A) := by
  rwa [red.advantage_eq A]

end PerfectReduction

namespace DecisionGame

/-- **Approximate game-hop theorem.** If corresponding worlds of two games are
within `δfalse` and `δtrue` in `ℓ¹` distance, then every deterministic
adversary's target advantage is at most its source advantage plus those two
simulation errors. -/
theorem advantage_le_of_world_gaps {Ω : Type*} [Fintype Ω]
    (source target : DecisionGame Ω) (A : Ω → Bool) (δfalse δtrue : ℝ)
    (hfalse : LWEOperational.l1Gap
      (target.experiment.challenge false)
      (source.experiment.challenge false) ≤ δfalse)
    (htrue : LWEOperational.l1Gap
      (target.experiment.challenge true)
      (source.experiment.challenge true) ≤ δtrue) :
    target.advantage A ≤ source.advantage A + δfalse + δtrue := by
  have hf := LWEOperational.boolean_distinguisher_advantage
    (target.experiment.challenge false)
    (source.experiment.challenge false) A
  have ht := LWEOperational.boolean_distinguisher_advantage
    (target.experiment.challenge true)
    (source.experiment.challenge true) A
  have htriangle :
      |target.acceptance true A - target.acceptance false A| ≤
        |source.acceptance true A - source.

equivalence is executable, while `mass_preserving` states exact simulation of

structure PerfectReduction (source : DecisionGame Source)
    (target : DecisionGame Target) where
  transcriptEquiv : Source ≃ Target
  mass_preserving : ∀ (b : Bool) (x : Source),
    (target.experiment.challenge b).mass (transcriptEquiv x) =
      (source.experiment.challenge b).mass x

namespace PerfectReduction

variable {source : DecisionGame Source} {target : DecisionGame Target}

/-- Turn a target-game distinguisher into a source-game distinguisher. -/
def reduce (red : PerfectReduction source target) (A : Target → Bool) : Source → Bool :=
  A ∘ red.transcriptEquiv

/-- Perfect simulation preserves acceptance probability in each challenge world. -/
theorem acceptance_eq (red : PerfectReduction source target)
    (A : Target → Bool) (b : Bool) :
    source.acceptance b (red.reduce A) = target.acceptance b A := by
  rw [DecisionGame.acceptance, DecisionGame.acceptance]
  simp only [Finset.sum_filter]
  rw [← Equiv.sum_comp red.transcriptEquiv
    (fun y => if A y = true then (target.experiment.challenge b).mass y else 0)]
  apply Finset.sum_congr rfl
  intro x _
  simp only [reduce, Function.comp_apply]
  split_ifs with h
  · rw [red.mass_preserving]
  · rfl

/-- **Exact reduction theorem.** Every target distinguisher has exactly the same
advantage after reduction to the source multilinear Diffie--Hellman game. -/
theorem advantage_eq (red : PerfectReduction source target) (A : Target → Bool) :
    source.advantage (red.reduce A) = target.advantage A := by
  simp only [DecisionGame.advantage]
  rw [red.acceptance_eq A true, red.acceptance_eq A false]

/-- **Multilinear Diffie--Hellman hardness transfer.** If all source-game
adversaries have advantage at most `ε`, then all target graded-encoding
adversaries do as well. -/
theorem hardness_transfer (red : PerfectReduction source target) (ε : ℝ)
    (sourceHard : ∀ B : Source → Bool, source.advantage B ≤ ε) :
    ∀ A : Target → Bool, target.advantage A ≤ ε := by
  intro A
  rw [← red.advantage_eq A]
  exact sourceHard (red.reduce A)

/-- A strict target-game advantage yields a strict source-game advantage, the
contrapositive form used to turn an attack into an MDH solver. -/
theorem attack_to_source (red : PerfectReduction source target) (ε : ℝ)
    (A : Target → Bool) (attack : ε < target.advantage A) :
    ε < source.advantage (red.reduce A) := by
  rwa [red.advantage_eq A]

end PerfectReduction

namespace DecisionGame

/-- **Approximate game-hop theorem.** If corresponding worlds of two games are
within `δfalse` and `δtrue` in `ℓ¹` distance, then every deterministic
adversary's target advantage is at most its source advantage plus those two
simulation errors. -/
theorem advantage_le_of_world_gaps {Ω : Type*} [Fintype Ω]
    (source target : DecisionGame Ω) (A : Ω → Bool) (δfalse δtrue : ℝ)
    (hfalse : LWEOperational.l1Gap
      (target.experiment.challenge false)
      (source.experiment.challenge false) ≤ δfalse)
    (htrue : LWEOperational.l1Gap
      (target.experiment.challenge true)
      (source.experiment.challenge true) ≤ δtrue) :
    target.advantage A ≤ source.advantage A + δfalse + δtrue := by
  have hf := LWEOperational.boolean_distinguisher_advantage
    (target.experiment.challenge false)
    (source.experiment.challenge false) A
  have ht := LWEOperational.boolean_distinguisher_advantage
    (target.experiment.challenge true)
    (source.experiment.challenge true) A
  have htriangle :
      |target.acceptance true A - target.acceptance false A| ≤
        |source.acceptance true A - source.acceptance false A| +
        |target.acceptance false A - source.acceptance false A| +
        |target.acceptance true A - source.acceptance true A| := by
    calc
      |target.acceptance true A - target.acceptance false A| =
          |(source.acceptance true A - source.acceptance false A) +
            (target.acceptance true A - source.acceptance true A) +
            (source.acceptance false A - target.acceptance false A)| := by
              congr 1
              ring
      _ ≤ |source.acceptance true A - source.acceptance false A| +
            |target.acceptance true A - source.acceptance true A| +
            |source.acceptance false A - target.acceptance false A| :=
              abs_add_three _ _ _
      _ = |source.acceptance true A - source.acceptance false A| +
            |target.acceptance false A - source.acceptance false A| +
            |target.acceptance true A - source.acceptance true A| := by
              rw [abs_sub_comm (source.acceptance false A)]
              ring
  simp only [advantage, acceptance] at htriangle ⊢
  exact htriangle.trans (by linarith [hf.trans hfalse, ht.trans htrue])

/-- Hardness therefore transfers through an approximate simulator with additive
loss equal to the sum of its two world-simulation errors. -/
theorem approximate_hardness_transfer {Ω : Type*} [Fintype Ω]
    (source target : DecisionGame Ω) (ε δfalse δtrue : ℝ)
    (sourceHard : ∀ A : Ω → Bool, source.advantage A ≤ ε)
    (hfalse : LWEOperational.l1Gap
      (target.experiment.challenge false)
      (source.experiment.challenge false) ≤ δfalse)
    (htrue : LWEOperational.l1Gap
      (target.experiment.challenge true)
      (source.experiment.challenge true) ≤ δtrue) :
    ∀ A : Ω → Bool, target.advantage A ≤ ε + δfalse + δtrue := by
  intro A
  exact (advantage_le_of_world_gaps source target A δfalse δtrue hfalse htrue).trans
    (by linarith [sourceHard A])

end DecisionGame
end Cryptography.GradedEncoding

end

# Future Directions

The following conjectures are concrete extensions of the formal reduction layer.
Each can be falsified by a finite counterexample to its stated bound.

1. **Randomized-distinguisher lifting.** For every finite transcript type, replacing
   deterministic Boolean distinguishers by Markov kernels to `Bool` preserves the
   exact-advantage theorem for every `PerfectReduction`.

2. **Tight statistical loss.** For any two finite decision games on one transcript
   space and any deterministic distinguisher, the additive loss in
   `advantage_le_of_world_gaps` can be sharpened from the sum of the two `ℓ¹` gaps
   to half that sum when both challenge distributions have total mass one.

3. **Composable perfect reductions.** The identity transcript equivalence forms a
   perfect reduction, perfect reductions compose, and the induced `reduce`
   operation is functorial; in particular, exact advantage preservation remains
   exact after any finite chain of reductions.

4. **Hybrid-chain bound.** Given `n + 1` finite games on a common transcript space
   whose adjacent corresponding-world `ℓ¹` gaps are bounded by `δ i b`, every
   Boolean distinguisher's endpoint advantage differs by at most
   `∑ i : Fin n, (δ i false + δ i true)`.

5. **Canonical graded evaluation coherence.** For every `System` and every binary
   parenthesization of a list of canonical level-one encodings, graded
   multiplication yields the canonical encoding of the plaintext product at the
   total level (after transporting along the induced equality of natural-number
   level expressions).

-- NEW_FILE: output-final_aristotle/Catalog/Bridges/CategoryTheoreticNeuralArchitectures.lean
import Mathlib
import Bridges.NeuralCompositionBridge
import Bridges.TannakianNeuralArchitecture

/-!
# Category-Theoretic Neural Architectures

This file models a neural architecture with input object `X` and output object `Y`
as a morphism `X ⟶ Y`.  The ambient cartesian monoidal category supplies parallel
composition.  Three precise bridges are established:

* a residual skip branch is the universal product lift of the identity and residual
  branch, and the usual ResNet block is obtained by following that lift with addition;
* two-head attention, represented by swapping two feature streams, is a natural
  transformation;
* finite architecture search over natural transformations is minimization over a
  hom-set of the functor category.

The analytic certification theorem reuses `NeuralCompositionBridge.lipschitz_add`,
and architecture search can carry the existing
`TannakianNeural.FeedforwardArchitecture` topology rather than introducing a new
notion of feedforward architecture.
-/

noncomputable section

open CategoryTheory CategoryTheory.Limits

namespace CategoryTheoreticNeuralArchitectures

universe v u

/-- Neural architectures are morphisms in their ambient category. -/
abbrev NeuralArchitecture (C : Type u) [Category.{v} C] (X Y : C) := X ⟶ Y

/-- Sequential composition of neural architectures is categorical composition. -/
def NeuralArchitecture.then {C : Type u} [Category.{v} C] {X Y Z : C}
    (f : NeuralArchitecture C X Y) (g : NeuralArchitecture C Y Z) :
    NeuralArchitecture C X Z := f ≫ g

/-- Parallel composition in a cartesian monoidal category is the canonical product map. -/
def NeuralArchitecture.parallel {C : Type u} [Category.{v} C]
    {X₁ X₂ Y₁ Y₂ : C} [HasBinaryProduct X₁ X₂] [HasBinaryProduct Y₁ Y₂]
    (f : NeuralArchitecture C X₁ Y₁) (g : NeuralArchitecture C X₂ Y₂) :
    NeuralArchitecture C (X₁ ⨯ X₂) (Y₁ ⨯ Y₂) :=
  prod.map f g

/-! ## Residual connections as categorical products -/

/-- The categorical skip connection pairs the unchanged input with its residual branch. -/
def resNetSkip {C : Type u} [Category.{v} C] {X : C} [HasBinaryProduct X X]
    (residual : X ⟶ X) : X ⟶ X ⨯ X :=
  prod.lift (𝟙 X) residual

/-- The first projection of a residual product is exactly the identity skip branch. -/
theorem resNetSkip_fst {C : Type u} [Category.{v} C] {X : C} [HasBinaryProduct X X]
    (residual : X ⟶ X) :
    resNetSkip residual ≫ prod.fst = 𝟙 X :=
  prod.lift_fst _ _

/-- The second projection of a residual product is exactly the learned branch. -/
theorem resNetSkip_snd {C : Type u} [Category.{v} C] {X : C} [HasBinaryProduct X X]
    (residual : X ⟶ X) :
    resNetSkip residual ≫ prod.snd = residual :=
  prod.lift_snd _ _

/-- The skip connection is uniquely determined by its identity and residual projections.
This is the categorical product universal property, not merely a representation by pairs. -/
theorem resNetSkip_unique {C : Type u} [Category.{v} C] {X : C} [HasBinaryProduct X X]
    (residual : X ⟶ X) (candidate : X ⟶ X ⨯ X)
    (hskip : candidate ≫ prod.fst = 𝟙 X)
    (hresidual : candidate ≫ prod.snd = residual) :
    candidate = resNetSkip residual := by
  apply prod.hom_ext
  · simpa [resNetSkip] using hskip
  · simpa [resNetSkip] using hresidual

/-- The usual additive readout of the identity and residual branches.  The two
branches are characterized categorically by `resNetSkip_fst` and `resNetSkip_snd`. -/
def resNetBlock {E : Type u} [Add E] (residual : E → E) : E → E :=
  fun x => x + residual x

/-- The categorical product realization is compatible with the catalog's analytic
certificate: a `K`-Lipschitz residual branch gives a `(1+K)`-Lipschitz block. -/
theorem resNet_product_lipschitz {E : Type u} [SeminormedAddCommGroup E]
    {K : NNReal} {residual : E → E} (hresidual : LipschitzWith K residual) :
    LipschitzWith (1 + K) (resNetBlock residual) :=
  NeuralCompositionBridge.lipschitz_add LipschitzWith.id hresidual

/-! ## Attention as a natural transformation -/

/-- Two parallel feature streams associated to a representation functor. -/
def twoHeadFeatures {C : Type u} [Category.{v} C] (F : C ⥤ Type u) : C ⥤ Type u where
  obj X := F.obj X × F.obj X
  map f p := (F.map f p.1, F.map f p.2)
  map_id X := by
    funext p
    simp

as a morphism `X ⟶ Y`.  The ambient cartesian monoidal category supplies parallel
composition.  Three precise bridges are established:

* a residual skip branch is the universal product lift of the identity and residual
  branch, and the usual ResNet block is obtained by following that lift with addition;
* two-head attention, represented by swapping two feature streams, is a natural
  transformation;
* finite architecture search over natural transformations is minimization over a
  hom-set of the functor category.

and architecture search can carry the existing
`TannakianNeural.FeedforwardArchitecture` topology rather than introducing a new
notion of feedforward architecture.

open CategoryTheory CategoryTheory.Limits

namespace CategoryTheoreticNeuralArchitectures

universe v u

/-- Neural architectures are morphisms in their ambient category. -/
abbrev NeuralArchitecture (C : Type u) [Category.{v} C] (X Y : C) := X ⟶ Y

/-- Sequential composition of neural architectures is categorical composition. -/
def NeuralArchitecture.then {C : Type u} [Category.{v} C] {X Y Z : C}
    (f : NeuralArchitecture C X Y) (g : NeuralArchitecture C Y Z) :
    NeuralArchitecture C X Z := f ≫ g

/-- Parallel composition in a cartesian monoidal category is the canonical product map. -/
def NeuralArchitecture.parallel {C : Type u} [Category.{v} C]
    {X₁ X₂ Y₁ Y₂ : C} [HasBinaryProduct X₁ X₂] [HasBinaryProduct Y₁ Y₂]
    (f : NeuralArchitecture C X₁ Y₁) (g : NeuralArchitecture C X₂ Y₂) :
    NeuralArchitecture C (X₁ ⨯ X₂) (Y₁ ⨯ Y₂) :=
  prod.map f g

/-! ## Residual connections as categorical products -/

/-- The categorical skip connection pairs the unchanged input with its residual branch. -/
def resNetSkip {C : Type u} [Category.{v} C] {X : C} [HasBinaryProduct X X]
    (residual : X ⟶ X) : X ⟶ X ⨯ X :=
  prod.lift (𝟙 X) residual

/-- The first projection of a residual product is exactly the identity skip branch. -/
theorem resNetSkip_fst {C : Type u} [Category.{v} C] {X : C} [HasBinaryProduct X X]
    (residual : X ⟶ X) :
    resNetSkip residual ≫ prod.fst = 𝟙 X :=
  prod.lift_fst _ _

/-- The second projection of a residual product is exactly the learned branch. -/

    (residual : X ⟶ X) :
    resNetSkip residual ≫ prod.snd = residual :=
  prod.lift_snd _ _

    (residual : X ⟶ X) (candidate : X ⟶ X ⨯ X)
    (hskip : candidate ≫ prod.fst = 𝟙 X)
    (hresidual : candidate ≫ prod.snd = residual) :
    candidate = resNetSkip residual := by
  apply prod.hom_ext
  · simpa [resNetSkip] using hskip
  · simpa [resNetSkip] using hresidual

concept.title: EML Interpolation Theory: Stone-Weierstrass for exp-log Networks
concept.concept_description: The Stone-Weierstrass theorem guarantees that any continuous function can be approximated by an algebra that separates points and contains constants. Conjecture: The algebra of EML functions (finite compositions of exp, log, +, *) on any compact subset of R^n is dense in C(K) with a Jackson-type rate: for f in Lip_alpha(K), there exists an EML network of width O(epsilon^{-n/alpha}) approximating f within epsilon. The separation property is key: given x != y in K, the function g(t) = exp(a)*log(b*t + c) can separate them for appropriate parameters a, b, c (because g is strictly monotone for a, b > 0). The constants are included via c = exp(a)*log(c) for c > 0. This gives EML networks provable approximation guarantees with explicit rates, going beyond the existential guarantees of universal approximation theorems. Test: prove the separation property (given x != y in K, find EML parameters that separate them) and the rate bound for Lipschitz functions. Construct an EML network of width n approximating x^2 on [0,1] with explicit error bounds. Impact: gives EML networks provable approximation guarantees with explicit rates, surpassing the existential guarantees of universal approximation theorems.

## Concept

**Title**: EML Interpolation Theory: Stone-Weierstrass for exp-log Networks
**Domain**: Applications
**Mathematical framing**: The Stone-Weierstrass theorem guarantees that any continuous function can be approximated by an algebra that separates points and contains constants. Conjecture: The algebra of EML functions (finite compositions of exp, log, +, *) on any compact subset of R^n is dense in C(K) with a Jackson-type rate: for f in Lip_alpha(K), there exists an EML network of width O(epsilon^{-n/alpha}) approximating f within epsilon. The separation property is key: given x != y in K, the function g(t) = exp(a)*log(b*t + c) can separate them for appropriate parameters a, b, c (because g is strictly monotone for a, b > 0). The constants are included via c = exp(a)*log(c) for c > 0. This gives EML networks provable approximation guarantees with explicit rates, going beyond the existential guarantees of universal approximation theorems. Construct an EML network of width n approximating x^2 on [0,1] with explicit error bounds. import Mathlib

/-! # EML interpolation: analysis, topology, and network complexity

This file gives a precise bridge from exp--log expressions to Stone--Weierstrass
approximation.  It also records explicit finite-width realizations of the square
function.  The quantitative Jackson conjecture is deliberately separated from the
proved density result: Stone--Weierstrass alone does not supply a width rate.
-/

noncomputable section

open Real Set

namespace EMLInterpolationTheory

/-- A one-neuron exp--log feature with affine input. -/
def logFeature (a b c t : ℝ) : ℝ := Real.exp a * Real.log (b * t + c)

/-- The proposed exp--log feature really separates any two real points, with a
positive slope and with both logarithm arguments in their natural positive domain. -/
theorem logFeature_separates {x y : ℝ} (hxy : x ≠ y) :
    ∃ a b c : ℝ,
      0 < b ∧ 0 < b * x + c ∧ 0 < b * y + c ∧
        logFeature a b c x ≠ logFeature a b c y := by
  use 0, 1, |x| + |y| + 1
  refine ⟨by norm_num, ?_, ?_, ?_⟩
  · cases abs_cases x <;> cases abs_cases y <;> linarith
  · cases abs_cases x <;> cases abs_cases y <;> linarith
  · simp [logFeature]
    show ¬(log (x + (|x| + |y| + 1)) = log (y + (|x| + |y| + 1)))
    have posx : x + (|x| + |y| + 1) > 0 := by cases abs_cases x <;> cases abs_cases y <;> linarith
    have posy : y + (|x| + |y| + 1) > 0 := by cases abs_cases x <;> cases abs_cases y <;> linarith
    exact fun h => hxy (by linarith [Real.log_injOn_pos (x₁ := x + (|x| + |y| + 1)) (x₂ := y + (|x| + |y| + 1)) posx posy h])

/-- Coordinatewise version: one exp--log neuron separates two vectors.  This is the
finite-dimensional geometric input to Stone--Weierstrass. -/
theorem logFeature_separates_vectors {n : ℕ} {x y : Fin n → ℝ} (hxy : x ≠ y) :
    ∃ i : Fin n, ∃ a b c : ℝ,
      0 < b ∧ 0 < b * x i + c ∧ 0 < b * y i + c ∧
        logFeature a b c (x i) ≠ logFeature a b c (y i) := by
  have ⟨i, hi⟩ := Function.ne_iff.mp hxy
  obtain ⟨a, b, c, hb, hx, hy, hne⟩ := logFeature_separates hi
  exact ⟨i, a, b, c, hb, hx, hy, hne⟩

section StoneWeierstrass

variable {n : ℕ} (K : Set (Fin n → ℝ)) [CompactSpace K]

/-- Exponentiating a coordinate gives a continuous EML feature on a compact set. -/
def coordinateExp (i : Fin n) : C(K, ℝ) where
  toFun x := Real.exp (x.1 i)
  continuous_toFun :=
    Real.continuous_exp.comp ((continuous_apply i).comp continuous_subtype_val)

omit [CompactSpace K] in
/-- The algebra generated by coordinate exponential features separates points. -/
theorem coordinateExp_adjoin_separates :
    (Algebra.adjoin ℝ (Set.range (coordinateExp K))).SeparatesPoints := by
  intro x y hxy
  have hne : x.1 ≠ y.1 := Subtype.coe_ne_coe.mpr hxy
  obtain ⟨i, hi⟩ : ∃ i : Fin n, x.1 i ≠ y.1 i := Function.ne_iff.mp hne
  refine ⟨coordinateExp K i, ?_, ?_⟩
  · exact Set.mem_image_of_mem _ (Algebra.subset_adjoin (Set.mem_range_self i))
  · intro heq
    exact hi (Real.exp_injective heq)

/-- **EML--Stone--Weierstrass connector.**  Finite algebraic combinations of
coordinate exponentials are dense in all real continuous functions on every compact
subset of finite-dimensional Euclidean space. -/
theorem coordinateExp_adjoin_dense :
    (Algebra.adjoin ℝ (Set.range (coordinateExp K))).topologicalClosure = ⊤ := by
  exact ContinuousMap.subalgebra_topologicalClosure_eq_top_of_separatesPoints _
    (coordinateExp_adjoin_separates K)

end StoneWeierstrass

/-! ## A concrete expression language and explicit square networks -/

/-- Finite EML expression trees. -/
inductive Expr where
  | const (c : ℝ)
  | var
  | exp (e : Expr)
  | log (e : Expr)
  | add (e₁ e₂ : Expr)
  | mul (e₁ e₂ : Expr)
  deriving Inhabited

namespace Expr

/-- Evaluation of an EML expression. -/
noncomputable def eval : Expr → ℝ → ℝ
  | .const c, _ => c
  | .var, x => x
  | .exp e, x => Real.exp (eval e x)
  | .log e, x => Real.log (eval e x)
  | .add e₁ e₂, x => eval e₁ x + eval e₂ x
  | .mul e₁ e₂, x => eval e₁ x * eval e₂ x

/-- Width is the number of leaves of the expression tree. -/
def width : Expr → ℕ
  | .const _ => 1
  | .var => 1
  | .exp e => width e
  | .log e => width e
  | .add e₁ e₂ => width e₁ + width e₂
  | .mul e₁ e₂ => width e₁ + width e₂

/-- Add `m` harmless zero leaves to an expression. -/
def padZero : ℕ → Expr → Expr
  | 0, e => e
  | m + 1, e => .add (.const 0) (padZero m e)

@[simp] theorem eval_padZero (m : ℕ) (e : Expr) (x : ℝ) :
    (padZero m e).eval x = e.eval x := by
  induction m with
  | zero => rfl
  | succ m ih =>
    show (padZero (m + 1) e).eval x = e.eval x
    simp only [padZero, Expr.eval]
    rw [ih]
    simp

@[simp] theorem width_padZero (m : ℕ) (e : Expr) :
    (padZero m e).width = e.width + m := by
  induction m with
  | zero => simp [padZero]
  | succ m ih => rw [padZero, width, width, ih]; ring

/-- The direct multiplication realization of the square. -/
def square : Expr := .mul .var .var

/-- For every requested width `n ≥ 2`, there is an EML expression of exactly that
width which computes `x²` on `[0,1]` (indeed, on all of `ℝ`), so its uniform error is
zero. -/
theorem square_exact_at_width {n : ℕ} (hn : 2 ≤ n) :
    ∃ e : Expr, e.width = n ∧
      ∀ x ∈ Set.Icc (0 : ℝ) 1, |e.eval x - x ^ 2| = 0 := by
  refine ⟨padZero (n - 2) square, ?_, ?_⟩
  · simp [square, width, Nat.add_sub_of_le hn]
  · intro x _
    simp [square, eval, pow_two]

/-- A genuinely exp--log realization, shifted so that `log` is only evaluated at
positive arguments on `[0,1]`. -/
def shiftedExpLogSquare (δ : ℝ) : Expr :=
  .exp (.mul (.const 2) (.log (.add .var (.const δ))))

/-- Explicit error bound for the shifted exp--log square network.  Its output is
`(x+δ)²`, hence the error on `[0,1]` is at most `2δ+δ²`. -/
theorem shiftedExpLogSquare_error {δ : ℝ} (hδ : 0 < δ) :
    ∀ x ∈ Set.Icc (0 : ℝ) 1,
      |(shiftedExpLogSquare δ).eval x - x ^ 2| ≤ 2 * δ + δ ^ 2 := by
  intro x hx
  -- unfold the definition and simplify
  simp [shiftedExpLogSquare, Expr.eval]
  -- now we need: |exp(2 * log(x + δ)) - x²| ≤ 2δ + δ²
  -- since x + δ > 0, exp(2 * log(x + δ)) = (x + δ)²
  have hxδ : x + δ > 0 := by linarith [hx.1]
  have hexp : Real.exp (2 * Real.log (x + δ)) = (x + δ) ^ 2 := by
    rw [two_mul, Real.exp_add, Real.exp_log hxδ]
    ring
  rw [hexp]
  -- now: |(x + δ)² - x²| ≤ 2δ + δ²
  have h1 : (x + δ) ^ 2 - x ^ 2 = 2 * x * δ + δ ^ 2 := by ring
  rw [h1]
  rw [abs_of_nonneg]
  · -- 2 * x * δ + δ² ≤ 2δ + δ² iff x ≤ 1 (since δ > 0)
    have hx1 : x ≤ 1 := hx.2
    nlinarith
  · -- 2 * x * δ + δ² ≥ 0 since x ≥ 0, δ > 0
    nlinarith [hx.1]

/-- Choosing `δ ≤ ε/3` (and `δ ≤ 1`) turns the explicit estimate into an
`ε`-approximation. -/
theorem shiftedExpLogSquare_epsilon {ε δ : ℝ}
    (hδ : 0 < δ) (hδone : δ ≤ 1) (hδε : 3 * δ ≤ ε) :
    ∀ x ∈ Set.Icc (0 : ℝ) 1,
      |(shiftedExpLogSquare δ).eval x - x ^ 2| ≤ ε := by
  intro x hx
  calc
    |(shiftedExpLogSquare δ).eval x - x ^ 2| ≤ 2 * δ + δ ^ 2 :=
      shiftedExpLogSquare_error hδ x hx
    _ ≤ 3 * δ := by nlinarith [hδ.le]
    _ ≤ ε := hδε

end Expr

end EMLInterpolationTheory

# Future directions

## Quantitative approximation rates

`Catalog/Bridges/EMLInterpolationTheory.lean` proves the qualitative bridge supplied
by Stone–Weierstrass: on a compact subset of `ℝⁿ`, the algebra generated by coordinate
exponentials is dense in the continuous real-valued functions.  This theorem does
**not** imply the proposed Jackson width bound.  Establishing a rate of order
`O(ε⁻ⁿ/α)` requires additional quantitative ingredients:

1. formalize Hölder classes on compact subsets of `ℝⁿ`;
2. construct a grid or partition-of-unity interpolant with mesh size comparable to
   `(ε/C)^(1/α)`;
3. realize each local basis function by the selected EML architecture while tracking
   both uniform error and width;
4. distinguish expression-tree width, number of hidden units, number of parameters,
   and depth, since rates for one notion do not automatically transfer to another;
5. combine the local errors without losing the desired dimensional exponent.

Mathlib contains qualitative Bernstein and Stone–Weierstrass approximation results,
but the needed multivariate Hölder-to-network width estimate is not an immediate
corollary of those results.

## Architecture-sensitive lower and upper bounds

Because the expression language allows multiplication and the input variable, `x²`
has an exact width-two realization.  The file also proves an explicit shifted
exp–log realization whose error is at most `2δ + δ²` on `[0,1]`.  Future work should
fix a narrower neural architecture (for example, a single hidden layer of features
`exp(a) log(bx+c)`) before claiming nontrivial width bounds.  Otherwise algebraic
operations can make polynomial test cases exact at constant width.

Useful next targets are:

- a normal-form theorem translating generated-algebra terms into a specified network;
- continuity and positivity invariants ensuring every logarithm receives a positive
  input on the approximation domain;
- matching lower bounds for restricted depth or restricted coefficients;
- a multivariate exact representation theorem for quadratic forms;
- quantitative stability bounds under composition of `exp` and `log`.

## Computational evidence

No separate numerical evidence file is included.  The primary claims proved here are
symbolic identities, inequalities, and topological density statements rather than a
finite conjectural sequence.  Small floating-point tests would not validate the
Stone–Weierstrass conclusion, while the square error formula is established exactly
in Lean for every point of the interval.  Computational experiments would become
useful after choosing a restricted architecture and an optimization procedure for the
unproved Jackson-rate program.

/-- Explicit error bound for the shifted exp--log square network.  Its output is
`(x+δ)²`, hence the error on `[0,1]` is at most `2δ+δ²`. -/
theorem shiftedExpLogSquare_error {δ : ℝ} (hδ : 0 < δ) :
    ∀ x ∈ Set.Icc (0 : ℝ) 1,
      |(shiftedExpLogSquare δ).eval x - x ^ 2| ≤ 2 * δ + δ ^ 2 := by
  intro x hx
  -- unfold the definition and simplify
  simp [shiftedExpLogSquare, Expr.eval]
  -- now we need: |exp(2 * log(x + δ)) - x²| ≤ 2δ + δ²
  -- since x + δ > 0, exp(2 * log(x + δ)) = (x + δ)²
  have hxδ : x + δ > 0 := by linarith [hx.1]
  have hexp : Real.exp (2 * Real.log (x + δ)) = (x + δ) ^ 2 := by
    rw [two_mul, Real.exp_add, Real.exp_log hxδ]
    ring
  rw [hexp]
  -- now: |(x + δ)² - x²| ≤ 2δ + δ²
  have h1 : (x + δ) ^ 2 - x ^ 2 = 2 * x * δ + δ ^ 2 := by ring
  rw [h1]
  rw [abs_of_nonneg]
  · -- 2 * x * δ + δ² ≤ 2δ + δ² iff x ≤ 1 (since δ > 0)
    have hx1 : x ≤ 1 := hx.2
    nlinarith
  · -- 2 * x * δ + δ² ≥ 0 since x ≥ 0, δ > 0
    nlinarith [hx.1]

/-- Choosing `δ ≤ ε/3` (and `δ ≤ 1`) turns the explicit estimate into an
`ε`-approximation. -/
theorem shiftedExpLogSquare_epsilon {ε δ : ℝ}
    (hδ : 0 < δ) (hδone : δ ≤ 1) (hδε : 3 * δ ≤ ε) :
    ∀ x ∈ Set.Icc (0 : ℝ) 1,
      |(shiftedExpLogSquare δ).eval x - x ^ 2| ≤ ε := by
  intro x hx
  calc
    |(shiftedExpLogSquare δ).eval x - x ^ 2| ≤ 2 * δ + δ ^ 2 :=
      shiftedExpLogSquare_error hδ x hx
    _ ≤ 3 * δ := by nlinarith [hδ.le]
    _ ≤ ε := hδε

end Expr

end EMLInterpolationTheory

# Future directions

## Quantitative approximation rates

`Catalog/Bridges/EMLInterpolationTheory.lean` proves the qualitative bridge supplied
by Stone–Weierstrass: on a compact subset of `ℝⁿ`, the algebra generated by coordinate
exponentials is dense in the continuous real-valued functions.  This theorem does
**not** imply the proposed Jackson width bound.  Establishing a rate of order
`O(ε⁻ⁿ/α)` requires additional quantitative ingredients:

1. formalize Hölder classes on compact subsets of `ℝⁿ`;
2. construct a grid or partition-of-unity interpolant with mesh size comparable to
   `(ε/C)^(1/α)`;
3. realize each local basis function by the selected EML architecture while tracking
   both uniform error and width;
4. distinguish expression-tree width, number of hidden units, number of parameters,
   and depth, since rates for one notion do not automatically transfer to another;
5. combine the local errors without losing the desired dimensional exponent.

Mathlib contains qualitative Bernstein and Stone–Weierstrass approximation results,
but the needed multivariate Hölder-to-network width estimate is not an immediate
corollary of those results.

## Architecture-sensitive lower and upper bounds

Because the expression language allows multiplication and the input variable, `x²`
has an exact width-two realization.  The file also proves an explicit shifted
exp–log realization whose error is at most `2δ + δ²` on `[0,1]`.  Future work should
fix a narrower neural architecture (for example, a single hidden layer of features
`exp(a) log(bx+c)`) before claiming nontrivial width bounds.  Otherwise algebraic
operations can make polynomial test cases exact at constant width.

Useful next targets are:

- a normal-form theorem translating generated-algebra terms into a specified network;
- continuity and positivity invariants ensuring every logarithm receives a positive
  input on the approximation domain;
- matching lower bounds for restricted depth or restricted coefficients;
- a multivariate exact representation theorem for quadratic forms;
- quantitative stability bounds under composition of `exp` and `log`.

## Computational evidence

No separate numerical evidence file is included.  The primary claims proved here are
symbolic identities, inequalities, and topological density statements rather than a
finite conjectural sequence.  Small floating-point tests would not validate the
Stone–Weierstrass conclusion, while the square error formula is established exactly
in Lean for every point of the interval.  Computational experiments would become
useful after choosing a restricted architecture and an optimization procedure for the
unproved Jackson-rate program.

concept.concept_description: Investigate the ArXiv paper 'Transformation Semigroup Perspective on the Magma Monoid' and formalize its key results. Abstract: The monoid of all binary operations was first introduced by H. S. Kim and J. Neggers in 2008. Since then, different aspects and applications of this monoid were studied, while several questions about its semigroup-theoretic properties remain unanswered. We employ a transformation semigroup perspective to fully characterize principal left and right ideals, idempotent and regular elements of this monoid, as well as provide precise combinatorial enumerations of them. -- NEW_FILE: output-final_aristotle/Tropical/MagmaMonoid/Transformation.lean
import Mathlib

/-!
# The magma monoid as a transformation monoid

A formalization of the pairmorph viewpoint from Baiduk and Kozerenko,
*Transformation Semigroup Perspective on the Magma Monoid* (2026).
-/

namespace MagmaMonoid

/-- A binary operation on `X`. -/
abbrev Operation (X : Type*) := X → X → X

/-- The product of binary operations defining the magma monoid. -/
def product {X : Type*} (f g : Operation X) : Operation X :=
  fun a b ↦ g (f a b) (f b a)

/-- The left-zero operation, which is the identity of the magma monoid. -/
def leftZero {X : Type*} : Operation X := fun a _ ↦ a

/-- The right-zero operation. -/
def rightZero {X : Type*} : Operation X := fun _ b ↦ b

/-- Reversal of an ordered pair. -/
def swap {X : Type*} (p : X × X) : X × X := (p.2, p.1)

/-- The pairmorph transformation induced by a binary operation. -/
def pairmorph {X : Type*} (f : Operation X) : X × X → X × X :=
  fun p ↦ (f p.1 p.2, f p.2 p.1)

/-- Transformations that commute with reversal of ordered pairs. -/
def IsPairmorph {X : Type*} (T : X × X → X × X) : Prop :=
  Function.Commute T swap

/-- The image of the pairmorph transformation. -/
def pairImage {X : Type*} (f : Operation X) : Set (X × X) :=
  Set.range (pairmorph f)

/-- The image under the pairmorph transformation of diagonal pairs. -/
def diagonalImage {X : Type*} (f : Operation X) : Set (X × X) :=
  Set.range (fun x ↦ pairmorph f (x, x))

/-- Diagonal points occurring anywhere in the pairmorph image. -/
def commutativeImage {X : Type*} (f : Operation X) : Set (X × X) :=
  pairImage f ∩ Set.range (fun x ↦ (x, x))

/-- Regularity in the magma monoid. -/
def IsRegular {X : Type*} (f : Operation X) : Prop :=
  ∃ g : Operation X, product (product f g) f = f

/-- The magma product is associative. -/
theorem product_assoc {X : Type*} (f g h : Operation X) :
    product (product f g) h = product f (product g h) := by
  funext a b
  simp [product]

/-- The left-zero operation is a left identity. -/
theorem leftZero_product {X : Type*} (f : Operation X) :
    product leftZero f = f := by
  funext a b
  simp [product, leftZero]

/-- The left-zero operation is a right identity. -/
theorem product_leftZero {X : Type*} (f : Operation X) :
    product f leftZero = f := by
  funext a b
  simp [product, leftZero]

/-- Pairmorph converts the magma product into composition of transformations. -/
theorem pairmorph_product {X : Type*} (f g : Operation X) :
    pairmorph (product f g) = pairmorph g ∘ pairmorph f := by
  funext p
  simp [product, pairmorph]

/-- Every pairmorph transformation commutes with pair reversal. -/
theorem pairmorph_commutes {X : Type*} (f : Operation X) :
    IsPairmorph (pairmorph f) := by
  simp [IsPairmorph, Function.Commute, Function.Semiconj]
  intro a b
  rfl

/-- A transformation is induced by a binary operation exactly when it commutes with
pair reversal (Lemma 2 of the paper). -/
theorem exists_pairmorph_iff {X : Type*} (T : X × X → X × X) :
    (∃ f : Operation X, pairmorph f = T) ↔ IsPairmorph T := by
  constructor
  · intro ⟨f, hf⟩
    rw [hf.symm]
    exact pairmorph_commutes f
  · intro hT
    use fun a b => (T (a, b)).1
    funext p
    simp only [pairmorph]
    have h := hT p
    simp only [swap] at h
    rw [h]

/-- Pairmorph faithfully represents binary operations. -/
theorem pairmorph_injective {X : Type*} :
    Function.Injective (pairmorph : Operation X → (X × X → X × X)) := by
  intro f g hfg
  funext a b
  have h := congr_arg Prod.fst (congr_fun hfg (a, b))
  simpa [pairmorph] using h

/-- Idempotents are exactly the operations whose pairmorph fixes every point of its
image (Proposition 20 of the paper). -/
theorem product_self_eq_iff {X : Type*} (f : Operation X) :
    product f f = f ↔ ∀ p ∈ pairImage f, pairmorph f p = p := by
  constructor
  · intro h p hp
    obtain ⟨q, rfl⟩ := hp
    have : pairmorph f (pairmorph f q) = (pairmorph f ∘ pairmorph f) q := rfl
    rw [this, ← pairmorph_product, h]
  · intro h
    funext a b
    have hp : (f a b, f b a) ∈ pairImage f := ⟨(a, b), rfl⟩
    have hf := h (f a b, f b a) hp
    simp [pairmorph] at hf
    exact hf.1

/-- Every commutative, pointwise-idempotent operation is an idempotent of the magma
monoid (Proposition 21 of the paper). -/
theorem commutative_idempotent_is_magma_idempotent {X : Type*} (f : Operation X)
    (hcomm : ∀ a b, f a b = f b a) (hidem : ∀ a, f a a = a) :
    product f f = f := by
